Checking calibration and how much to verify

Source: vignettes/calibration.Rmd
calibration.Rmd

A 95% credible interval should contain the true value in about 95% of datasets. When the model is misspecified, it may not, and nothing in a single fit will warn you. Simulation-based calibration answers the question for a given design: simulate many datasets from known parameters, fit the model to each, and count how often the intervals cover the truth. This is a coverage-based form of simulation-based calibration checking, one of the steps of the Bayesian workflow (Gelman et al., 2026, Ch. 31).

The workflow

  1. Describe the design you can afford: number of sites, automated occasions, fraction of sites verified, and plausible detection and false-positive rates.
  2. Describe the false-positive structure you suspect: homogeneous, random among sites, or tracking an environmental gradient.
  3. Run fp_calibrate() with the candidate models.
  4. Read the coverage and bias of the quantity you care about, usually the occupancy slope.
library(crywolf)
fp_compile()   # compile once before starting parallel workers

future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 8)

design <- expand.grid(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, frac_verified = 0.3,
  conf_effect = c(0, 0.5, 1.5), conf_cor = 0.7
)

cal <- fp_calibrate(
  design,
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  occ = ~ x, reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
summary(cal)

The code above is not run when this vignette is built; the output below comes from the same call, saved in advance. summary() prints, for the occupancy slope, the coverage of the 95% intervals, its Monte Carlo standard error, the bias, and a verdict:

#> Calibration summary (95% intervals)
#> 
#> Occupancy slope:
#>  cell    model nsite nocc  p10 frac_verified conf_effect conf_cor  n failed
#>     1 constant   300   20 0.05           0.3         0.0      0.7 50      0
#>     1  fp_on_x   300   20 0.05           0.3         0.0      0.7 50      0
#>     2 constant   300   20 0.05           0.3         0.5      0.7 50      0
#>     2  fp_on_x   300   20 0.05           0.3         0.5      0.7 50      0
#>     3 constant   300   20 0.05           0.3         1.5      0.7 50      0
#>     3  fp_on_x   300   20 0.05           0.3         1.5      0.7 50      0
#>  coverage mc_se    bias rmse prop_divergent   verdict

#>      0.98 0.020 -0.0081 0.13           0.00        ok
#>      0.96 0.028  0.0094 0.13           0.00        ok
#>      0.96 0.028 -0.0016 0.13           0.02        ok
#>      0.22 0.059  0.4090 0.44           0.00 collapsed
#>      0.62 0.069  0.2301 0.27           0.00 collapsed
#> 
#> All quantities: inspect the returned tibble.

Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the strength of the confusion, for the constant-rate model and for a false-positive rate that depends on the occupancy covariate. Bars span two Monte Carlo standard errors; the dashed line is the nominal coverage.

Each replicate costs one Stan fit per model, so this design needs 3 cells × 50 replicates × 2 models = 300 fits. With 50 replicates, the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage of 0.95 is about 0.03, enough to tell a calibrated model from a broken one; raise reps only to pin a borderline value. Every model is fitted to the same datasets, so comparisons between models are paired.

The column prop_divergent is the share of fits with at least one divergent transition. In this run only 2 of the 800 fits had one, and the largest R-hat was 1.01. Check max_rhat and divergences in the returned tibble before trusting a cell whose fits had many. The simulated designs here have no recorder effect, so the calibration fits leave the recorder random intercept out; fitting a random effect whose true variance is zero is a common source of divergent transitions.

How much to verify

Verification anchors the false-positive rate. It is natural to think that verifying more sites will rescue a model that is not calibrated, and fp_verification_curve() tests that directly:

fp_verification_curve(
  nsite = 300, nocc = 20, p10 = 0.05, conf_effect = 1.5, conf_cor = 0.7,
  frac_verified = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9),
  models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_on_x = ~ x),
  reps = 50, parallel = TRUE
)
#> Calibration summary (95% intervals)

Coverage of the 95% interval of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, under structured confusion (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7).

What to expect

In the simulation study that motivated this package (Provete et al., in preparation), at a base false-positive rate of 0.05:

  • When false positives were homogeneous, the constant-rate model kept nominal coverage of the occupancy slope. When they varied at random among sites, the estimate of the false-positive rate became unreliable, but coverage of the slope fell only to 0.81 (across all cells of that regime).
  • When the false-positive rate tracked a gradient correlated with the occupancy covariate (effect 1.5 on the logit scale, correlation 0.7), coverage of the slope fell to 0.08–0.20, and verifying up to 90% of the sites did not restore it.
  • Letting the false-positive rate depend on the occupancy covariate (fp = ~ x) recovered part of the coverage (0.48–0.66) and improved with verification; with the true gradient (fp = ~ w), coverage returned to 0.90–0.97.
  • Weak confusion (effects of 0.5 or less) left the constant-rate model calibrated at every correlation, including when false positives depended on the occupancy covariate itself.

So, if fp_verification_curve() shows the constant-rate model stuck below nominal coverage, verifying more is not the remedy. Model the false-positive rate instead, and verify enough to tell its effect apart from the occupancy effect.

Calibrating a fitted model

The checks above describe a planned design with simulated covariates. Once a model has been fitted to real data, fp_calibrate_fit() asks the same question for data like the real ones: it simulates datasets from the fit with simulate(), keeping the sites, covariates, occasions, recorders, and verification of the real data, refits each candidate model to every dataset, and scores the coverage and bias of their intervals. The cost is that of refitting the real data reps times per model.

A typical use pits the model you fitted against a simpler one. If a model in which the false-positive rate depends on humidity found a clear effect, data simulated from it show whether a constant rate would have biased the occupancy effects at your sample size and verification effort:

m_rh <- fp_occu(d, occ = ~ temp + rh, det = ~ bio, fp = ~ rh)
cal_fit <- fp_calibrate_fit(m_rh, models = list(constant = ~ 1, fp_rh = ~ rh),
                            reps = 50, parallel = TRUE)
summary(cal_fit)
plot(cal_fit, parameter = "occ_rh")

By default every dataset is simulated from the posterior means; truth = "posterior" draws a different set of parameter values from the posterior for each dataset, so that the check also reflects how uncertain the fit was. Either way, the check covers only the structure of the generating model: a dependence of the false-positive rate on a variable that was not measured is not part of it.

Plotting

plot() draws the coverage of the occupancy slope against the design column that varies (here, the fraction of sites verified), one colour per model, with intervals of two Monte Carlo standard errors and a dashed line at the nominal level. type = "bias" plots the bias instead, and parameter selects another scored quantity. The result is a ‘ggplot2’ object that can be modified as usual.

plot(cal)
plot(cal, type = "bias")
plot(cal, parameter = "p10_bar")

For the verification curve above, the bias of the occupancy slope shows why coverage stays low: the constant-rate model overestimates the slope at every level of verification, and modelling the rate on x reduces, but does not remove, the bias.

Bias of the posterior mean of the occupancy slope against the fraction of sites verified, under structured confusion (effect 1.5, correlation 0.7). The dashed line marks no bias.

Coverage of the 95% interval of the mean false-positive rate over sites (p10_bar), in the same simulations.

Neither model recovers the mean false-positive rate over sites under this confusion. Both estimate it at about 0.077 when the truth is about 0.10, with intervals only about 0.02 wide, so coverage stays at 0.22 or below at every level of verification. Modelling the rate on x reduces the bias of the occupancy slope, but a rate that depends on the unmeasured gradient w is not fully captured by x.

Gelman, A., Vehtari, A., McElreath, R., Simpson, D., Margossian, C. C., Yao, Y., Kennedy, L., Gabry, J., Bürkner, P.-C., Modrák, M., & Leos Barajas, V. (2026). Bayesian Workflow. Chapman & Hall. https://avehtari.github.io/Bayesian-Workflow/
